questions.question: The Arabic particle 'la' that opens the oath in verse 1 is understood by classical scholars in what way?
options: A negation meaning Allah declines to swear by the Day of Resurrection
An emphatic particle that adds solemnity and weight to the oath that follows
A conditional particle meaning 'if' the Day of Resurrection arrives
A rhetorical question inviting the listener to imagine the Day
questions.explanation: Imam al-Tabari, in Jami al-Bayan, affirms that the majority of the early Salaf understood 'la uqsimu' as an emphatic introducer rather than a negation, consistent with classical Arabic usage. The particle intensifies the oath rather than negating it.

questions.question: True or false: The phrase 'al-nafs al-lawwamah' appears in multiple surahs throughout the Quran.
questions.explanation: The phrase 'al-nafs al-lawwamah' appears only in this one verse in the entire Quran, making it unique to Surah al-Qiyamah. This singular appearance heightens its significance, as noted in the foundation layer tafsir of this surah.

questions.question: According to al-Hasan al-Basri, as recorded by Ibn Kathir, what distinguishes the believer's nafs al-lawwamah from the attitude of the sinner?
options: The believer reproaches himself over his intentions and words, while the sinner presses forward without self-blame
The believer's soul never experiences reproach because sincere faith protects it from guilt
The sinner reproaches more intensely because he is more aware of his wrongdoing
Both the believer and sinner experience equal self-reproach, but only the believer acts on it
questions.explanation: Al-Hasan al-Basri said, as recorded by Ibn Kathir: 'Verily, by Allah, we think that every believer blames himself, saying: what did I intend by my speech, what did I intend by my eating... But the sinner presses forward and does not blame himself.' This marks the reproaching soul as a sign of living faith.

questions.question: True or false: According to Imam al-Qurtubi, Allah's ability to reassemble bones requires the original atoms to be in a particular place or state.
questions.explanation: Imam al-Qurtubi, in Al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran, stresses that the Quraysh objection misunderstands divine omnipotence. Allah does not require the original atoms to be in any particular state in order to resurrect, because He creates from nothing. The same power that initiated creation governs re-creation.

questions.question: Why does verse 4 specifically mention the fingertips as the example of what Allah will reconstruct on the Day of Resurrection?
options: Because fingertips were considered the most spiritually significant part of the body in classical Arab culture
Because reconstructing the most intricate detail of the body proves Allah can reassemble the larger, more obvious structures
Because fingertips are the last part of the body to decompose after death
Because the Quraysh had challenged the Prophet specifically about the fate of fingertips
questions.explanation: Verse 4 uses a logical argument from greater to lesser: if Allah can reconstruct the delicate, ridged skin of a unique fingertip, reassembling the larger skeleton is clearly within His power. Ibn Uthaymeen described the opening 'bala' as one of the most emphatic divine affirmations in the Quran, cutting through all doubt with finality.

questions.question: Sayyid Qutb, reflecting on verse 5 in Fi Zilal al-Quran, describes denial of resurrection primarily as what kind of problem?
options: An intellectual problem caused by insufficient evidence for the afterlife
A cultural problem rooted in pre-Islamic Arabian tribal customs
A moral problem — a form of spiritual flight that silences the conscience so one can sin without the shadow of judgment
A linguistic problem arising from misreading the Quranic text
questions.explanation: Sayyid Qutb identifies verse 5 as one of the Quran's most penetrating statements about the psychology of disbelief. He argues that denial of the hereafter is often moral flight — a way of silencing the conscience so the person can press forward in sin without the shadow of accountability, rather than an honest intellectual conclusion.

questions.question: What was the concern that led the Prophet to recite along with the angel Gabriel during revelation, which the divine instruction in verses 16-17 addressed?
options: He feared Gabriel might make an error in the delivery of the words
He feared forgetting the words of the revelation if he did not repeat them immediately
He wanted the companions present to hear the revelation as it came down
He was responding to a challenge from the Quraysh who denied the revelation was genuine
questions.explanation: Imam al-Tabari, drawing on the narration of Ibn Abbas, explains that the Prophet would move his tongue and lips rapidly during revelation out of fear of forgetting. Verses 16-19 reassured him: Allah Himself undertook to collect and preserve the Quran in his heart, making the anxious simultaneous recitation unnecessary.

questions.question: True or false: Wahbah al-Zuhayli argues in Al-Tafsir al-Munir that rejecting the Sunnah as a source of Quranic interpretation is not only a legal error but also a theological one, because verse 19 records Allah's own promise to clarify the Quran through the Prophet.
questions.explanation: Al-Zuhayli argues that 'inna alayna bayanahu' establishes the prophetic hadith as the divinely promised clarificatory system for the Quran. Denying the Sunnah as an interpretive source therefore contradicts the fulfillment of Allah's own pledge recorded in this verse, making it a theological error beyond a merely juristic one.

questions.question: The Arabic word 'nadirah,' used for the believers' faces in verse 22, conveys which of the following?
options: Pale and calm, reflecting inner peace after the fear of judgment has passed
Fresh, luminous, and overflowing with vitality — a radiance like a flower in full bloom
Grave and solemn, as befits the seriousness of standing before Allah
Tearful with gratitude for having been forgiven of sins
questions.explanation: The tafsir explains that 'nadirah' comes from the root meaning to be fresh and blooming. It is not merely the absence of distress but a positive, overflowing luminosity. Ibn Kathir connects it to the Quranic usage of the same root for the freshness of a well-watered plant, and records that the Companions understood it as the outward expression of the soul's inner bliss.

questions.question: True or false: The Sunni scholarly consensus, based on verse 23 and authenticated hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, is that believers will see Allah with their own eyes in the Hereafter.
questions.explanation: Imam al-Tabari affirms categorically that 'ila rabbiha nazirah' means literally looking at their Lord with their eyes, transmitting this from the Companions without dissent. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith: 'You will see your Lord as you see the full moon — you will not be crowded in your seeing of Him,' calling this the consensus of the Companions, Successors, and scholars of the Salaf.

questions.question: Sheikh Muhammad al-Sha'rawi reflected that the image of the soul rising to the collarbones in verse 26 mirrors which broader human pattern?
options: The soul's gradual purification through acts of worship during a person's lifetime
The process by which divine judgment moves from small deeds to large ones
The human habit of believing we are in control throughout life, until the moment all control dissolves at death
The Prophet's description of the angel of death approaching from below and rising upward
questions.explanation: Sheikh al-Sha'rawi reflected that the soul's journey upward to the collarbones mirrors the entire journey of human denial — we spend our lives believing we are in control, yet in this moment all control dissolves. This reading connects the death scene directly to the surah's broader theme of human heedlessness and divine sovereignty.

questions.question: What is the theological purpose of Allah reminding man in the surah's closing verses that he was once a sperm-drop ('nutfah min maniy yumna')?
options: To shame man for his lowly beginning and discourage pride in worldly achievements
To establish that the same Creator who produced a conscious human being from something so small can certainly resurrect him
To warn man that his body will return to the same microscopic state after death
To prove that man has no free will, since his existence began as something entirely passive
questions.explanation: The tafsir explains that this verse invites man to trace back the chain of his own existence: a drop of fluid does not spontaneously produce a conscious, morally responsible human being. The same Allah who produced man from something so small is the One asking him to account for the life He gave — and can certainly recreate him. As Sayyid Qutb writes in Fi Zilal al-Quran, this reminder should produce awe at the Creator, not shame at one's origins.
